<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[en:Tawara Tōda Monogatari]][[id:Kisah Tawara Tōda]][[ru:Тавара Тода]][[sv:Tawara Toda]][[uk:Тавара Тода]]
{{Italic title}}
{{Short description|Japanese heroic fairy tale}}
[[Image:Kuniyoshi The Dragon Princess.jpg|thumb|240px|Dragon Woman and Tawara Tōda. Centipede of Mt. Mikami (above).{{right|{{small|―[[Utagawa Kuniyoshi]] 1845, ''Tokaidō gojūsantsui: Kusatsu''}}}}]]
[[Image:Yoshitoshi Fujiwara no Hidesato.jpg|thumb|200px|Hidesato aiming his shoot at the giant centipede.{{right|{{small|―{{ill|Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|en|Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|WD=Q467337|lt=Tsukioka Yoshitoshi}} 1890.}}}}]]

{{nihongo|'''''The Tale of Tawara Tōda'''''|俵藤太物語|'''''Tawara Tōda monogatari'''''}} is a Japanese heroic tale recounting the legendary exploits of {{ill|Fujiwara no Hidesato|en|Fujiwara no Hidesato|WD=Q1136623|lt=Fujiwara no Hidesato}}. It is part of the ''[[otogi-zōshi]]'' genre of tales dating to the [[:en:Edo Period|Edo Period]] or earlier. Some of the fabulous accounts are also told in the {{ill|Gunki monogatari|en|Gunki monogatari|WD=Q587327|lt=military pseudo-chronicle}}, ''[[Taiheiki]]'' (14th century).

Hidesato used a {{ill|Bow and arrow|en|Bow and arrow|WD=Q19827042|lt=Bow and arrow}} to kill a giant centipede (''{{ill|ōmukade|en|ōmukade|WD=Q60788646|lt=mukade}}'') wrapped around a mountain near {{ill|Lake Biwa|en|Lake Biwa|WD=Q200239|lt=Lake Biwa}}, fulfilling the request of a serpent at a bridge, which turned out to be a court lady (or Dragon King) from the underwater {{nihongo||龍宮城|[[Ryūgū-jō]]|extra2="Dragon Palace"}}. The hero was entertained at the palace and received rewards including armor and sword, and an inexhaustible bag of rice.{{efn|Or rice sack ({{illm|Tawara (container)|lt=''tawara''|ja|俵}}).}}

'''"My Lord Bag-O'-Rice"'''  is English-translated title of {{ill|Basil Hall Chamberlain|en|Basil Hall Chamberlain|WD=Q810029|lt=Basil Hall Chamberlain}}'s retelling, published as a {{ill|Fairy tale|en|Fairy tale|WD=Q699|lt=Fairy tale}} (1887). This was later followed by {{ill|Yei Theodora Ozaki|en|Yei Theodora Ozaki|WD=Q8051334|lt=Yei Theodora Ozaki}}'s translation "'''My Lord Bag of Rice'''" (1903) based on {{illm|Iwaya Sazanami|ja|巌谷小波}}'s retelling.

== Setting ==
The story is set in {{ill|Ōmi Province|en|Ōmi Province|WD=Q843882|lt=Ōmi Province}} ({{ill|Shiga Prefecture|en|Shiga Prefecture|WD=Q131358|lt=Shiga Prefecture}}), and begins with a large serpent lying on {{illm|Seta Bridge|ja|瀬田の唐橋}} on the brink of {{ill|Lake Biwa|en|Lake Biwa|WD=Q200239|lt=Lake Biwa}}. The serpent, which later assumes human form, conveys Hidesato to the Dragon Palace, which can be reached through the depths of this Lake.{{sfnp|Kimbrough|2018}}{{sfnp|Visser|1913|pp=191–192}}

There is a Shinto shrine near the Seta Bridge at Lake Biwa where people have venerated Tawara Tōda.{{sfnp|Visser|1913|p=191}}

== Personage ==
{{nihongo|Tawara Tōda|俵藤太|extra=lit. 'Rice-bag Tōda'}} is a name that plays a {{ill|pun|en|pun|WD=Q263668|lt=pun}} between ''[[Wikt:tawara|tawara]]'' meaning 'straw rice-bag; straw barrel' and {{nihongo||Tawara|田原}}, a {{ill|proper noun|en|proper noun|WD=Q147276|lt=proper name}} (which may be a {{ill|Japanese name|en|Japanese name|WD=Q877834|lt=person's name}} or a place name). It was the nickname given to the historical {{ill|Fujiwara no Hidesato|en|Fujiwara no Hidesato|WD=Q1136623|lt=Fujiwara no Hidesato}} who flourished in the first half of the 10th century and participated in the suppression of the rebel usurper {{ill|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado|2=en|3=Taira no Masakado|4=ja|5=平将門|6=de|7=Taira no Masakado|8=es|9=Taira no Masakado|10=fr|11=Taira no Masakado|lt=Taira no Masakado|WD=Q1207652|en|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado|2=en|3=Taira no Masakado|4=ja|5=平将門|6=de|7=Taira no Masakado|8=es|9=Taira no Masakado|10=fr|11=Taira no Masakado|lt=Taira no Masakado|WD=Q1207652|WD=Q1207652|lt=Taira no Masakado}}.<ref>{{harvp|Visser|1913|loc=p. 191, 192 and note 3}}</ref>

The nickname is sometimes styled "Tawara [no] Tōta".<ref name=foster/>

== Summary ==
The hero's centipede-slaying legend as contained in the ''Tawara Tōda monogatari'' ("The Tale of Tawara Tōda") was widely circulated and read during the early [[:en:Edo Period|Edo Period]] (17th century), when the text was being copied in picture scrolls (''[[:en:Emaki|Emaki]]'') and appearing in [[:en:Otogizōshi|Otogizōshi]] type woodblock-printed (and hand-copied) books.{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The Tawara Tōda story is not one of the 23 pieces listed in the more stringent definition of ''otogizōshi''. But it has been printed under the ''otogizōshi'' anthology.{{r|knbt19}} {{harvp|Araki|1981}} also discusses it as an ''otogizōshi'' narrative, in the broader sense.}}{{sfnp|Araki|1981|pp=1–2}}{{sfnp|Kimbrough|2018}} A summary of the ''monogatari'' version is as follows:

{{Block indent|1=
Fujiwara no Hidesato confronted the large serpent which lay on {{illm|Seta Bridge|ja|瀬田の唐橋}} in {{ill|Ōmi Province|en|Ōmi Province|WD=Q843882|lt=Ōmi Province}} disrupting travelers. Undaunted by this twelve horned snake measuring 200 feet,{{efn|20 ''jō'' ().}} the hero stepped on its back and crossed over, continuing onward. That night he was visited by a young woman who proclaimed to be the transformation of the serpent. Near {{ill|Lake Biwa|en|Lake Biwa|WD=Q200239|lt=Lake Biwa}} where she lived, a huge centipede took up residence on {{ill|Mount Mikami|en|Mount Mikami|WD=Q10865239|lt=Mount Mikami}}, and was devouring beasts and fish and even her own kindred.
}}
{{Block indent|1=Hidesato accepted her plea to eradicate this creature, and went to Seta. When the centipede came slinking down, it appeared as if two or three thousand torches were descending the mountain. Hidesato shot two arrows which failed to lodge, but when he laid spittle on the third arrow and prayed to his patron [[Hachiman]] deity it struck a grievous blow. Hidesato approached the creature{{Efn|Which had a head like an ox-demon (''[[gyūki]]'')}} and hacked it to pieces.{{Efn|Presumably with his heirloom sword which he had brought.}}
}}
{{Block indent|1=The dragon woman was elated and gave him magical gifts: undiminishing bolts of silk, inexhaustible rice bag, and a {{ill|Shakudō|en|Shakudō|WD=Q912435|lt=crimson copper}} pan of plenty (or "pot of alloyed gold and copper"{{sfnp|Dykstra|Kurata|2000|p=76}}). It was on account of the rice bag ({{illm|Tawara (container)|lt=''tawara''|ja|俵}}) that Hidesato received the nickname Tawara Tōda. The dragon woman took him to the Dragon-Palace ([[Ryūgū-jō|Ryūgū]]), where he was entertained and lavished with additional gifts from the Dragon King.{{Efn|The ''monogatari'' version elaborates that this was {{ill|Sāgara (Dragon King)|en|Sāgara (Dragon King)|WD=Q85804720|lt=Sāgara the Dragon King}} who (in {{ill|Buddhism|en|Buddhism|WD=Q748|lt=Buddhism}}) was one of the {{illm|Eight Great Dragon Kings|ja|八大竜王}} (among the {{ill|Eight Legions|en|Eight Legions|WD=Q1045328|lt=Eight Legions}}).}} Hidesato was given armor and sword, and a crimson copper bell. Hidesato subsequently donated this bell to {{ill|Mii-dera|en|Mii-dera|WD=Q1756307|lt=Mii-dera}} temple at the foot of {{ill|Mount Hiei|en|Mount Hiei|WD=Q748040|lt=Mount Hiei}}.{{sfnp|Araki|1981|p=2}}{{sfnp|Kimbrough|2018}}{{r|knbt19}}{{efn|A legend concerning {{ill|Benkei|en|Benkei|WD=Q316898|lt=Benkei}} is attached to the bell. See below.}}
}}

The ''monogatari'' version probably derives from earlier accounts of Hidesato's centipede slaying described in the 14th-century ''[[Taiheiki]]'', expanded with layers of legendary and religious (Buddhist) motifs.{{sfnp|Araki|1981|pp=3–4}} The above summary is not the entirety of ''Tawara Tōda monogatari'', which contains a second part where the hero triumphs over {{ill|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado|2=en|3=Taira no Masakado|4=ja|5=平将門|6=de|7=Taira no Masakado|8=es|9=Taira no Masakado|10=fr|11=Taira no Masakado|lt=Taira no Masakado|WD=Q1207652|en|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado|2=en|3=Taira no Masakado|4=ja|5=平将門|6=de|7=Taira no Masakado|8=es|9=Taira no Masakado|10=fr|11=Taira no Masakado|lt=Taira no Masakado|WD=Q1207652|WD=Q1207652|lt=Taira no Masakado}}, despite the latter having an iron body which was invulnerable except at the {{ill|Temple (anatomy)|en|Temple (anatomy)|WD=Q243999|lt=temples}} on his head, and having six ghostly doubles of himself.{{sfnp|Araki|1981|pp=3–4}}

=== Taiheiki version ===
The 14th-century ''[[Taiheiki]]'' records a much earlier version of this legend about Hidesato,<ref>''Taiheiki'', Book 15 [[:ja:s:太平記/巻第十五|太平記 巻第十五]], Chapter 118 "About the Battle of Miidera Temple, etc. 三井寺合戦並当寺撞鐘事付俵藤太事".</ref>{{sfnp|Dykstra|Kurata|2000|p=61}} but instead of the dragon turning into a beautiful woman, it transforms into a "strange small man"{{sfnp|Dykstra|Kurata|2000|p=61}} – the {{ill|Dragon King|en|Dragon King|WD=Q135337914|lt=Dragon King}} himself.{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|In the ''Taiheiki'' it is not explcit that the "small man" and the "Dragon God" (not "Dragon King" in original text) are the same personage, so this must be inferred. The small man changes into wearing a {{nihongo||冠|kanmuri|extra2="crown"}} but this headdress is worn by various officials, not just the monarch.}}{{sfnp|Visser|1913|p=192}}{{r|shigehara}} And here, Hidesato is invited to the Dragon Palace first and thereafter combats the centipede that attacks the aquatic realm.{{sfnp|Dykstra|Kurata|2000|p=61}}{{sfnp|Friday|2008|pp=157-158}} Here the inexhaustible silk and rice bag are received from the Dragon King,{{efn|Rather than the Dragon Woman, as in the ''monogatari'' version}} but not the copper alloy pan/pot, only the copper temple-bell.{{sfnp|Friday|2008|pp=157-158}}

=== Other attestations ===
{{Further|Fujiwara no Hidesato#Legendary arms}}

A version (similar to the ''monogatari'') appears in {{Nihongo||本朝怪談故事|Honchō kaidan koji}} (1711) as pointed out by Dutch Japanologist {{illm|Marinus Willem de Visser|de|Marinus Willem de Visser}}.{{sfnp|Visser|1913|pp=191–192}}

The centipede coiled seven and a half turns around Mount Mikami according to popular tradition.{{r|foster}} An early written mention of this occurs in the {{ill|chorography|en|chorography|WD=Q2088593|lt=area guidebook}} ''Ōmi yochi shiryaku'' (1723).<ref>{{citation|last=Sangawa |first=Tokikiyo 寒川辰清 |script-title=ja:巻之卅九 秀郷社 |title=Book39: Hidesato (no) yashiro  |work=Ōmi yochi shiryaku 近江輿地志略 : 校定頭註 |publisher=Seinō Insatsu|year=1915|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/950934/284 |pages=466–468|language=ja}}</ref>

The name {{nihongo|Chikushi|遅来矢}} has been ascribed to the sword given by the Dragon King in the ''{{ill|Wakan Sansai Zue|en|Wakan Sansai Zue|WD=Q1135803|lt=Wakan sansai zue}}'' encyclopedia (1712) and the {{illm|Tōkaidō meisho zue|ja|東海道名所図会|lt=''Tōkaidō meisho zue''}} almanac (1797).{{Efn|This sword was passed down the {{illm|Akahori clan|ja|赤堀氏}}, these sources add.}}{{r|wakan-sansai-zue}}{{r|tokaido-meisho-zue}}<ref>Noted by {{harvp|Shida|1941|p=5}}</ref>

Hidesato's alleged armor from the Dragon Palace bore the similarly scripted name {{nihongo|Hiraishi|避来矢}} according to the ''Ujisatoki'' (before 1713{{r|owada}}).{{Efn|This armor was passed down {{illm|Sano clan|ja|佐野氏}} of {{ill|Shimotsuke Province|en|Shimotsuke Province|WD=Q1053699|lt=Shimotsuke Province}}, the ''Ujisatoki'' adds.}}<ref>{{harvp|Shida|1941|p=7}}: "the characters are extremely similar 文字が甚だよく似てゐる"</ref>{{r|ujisatoki-kondo}}<ref>Noted by {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|en|Minakata Kumagusu|WD=Q6862791|lt=Minakata Kumagusu}} (1916) ''[https://www.aozora.gr.jp/cards/000093/files/1916_29070.html Jūnishikō: Tawara Tōda ryūgū-iri no hanashi 十二支考 田原藤太竜宮入りの話]''; {{harvp|Nakamura|1971|p=214}}</ref> {{nihongo|Hiraishi|平石}}, an armor with the {{ill|Homophone|en|Homophone|WD=Q221079|lt=same-sounding}} but differently written name, is listed as a gift of Dragon Palace in [[Arai Hakuseki]]'s ''Honchō gunkikō'' (1709); this work mentions a second armor {{nihongo|Muromaru|室丸}} being obtained as well.{{r|honcho-gunkiko-armour}}<ref>Noted by {{harvp|Shida|1941|p=7}}; {{harvp|Nakamura|1971|p=214}}.</ref>

Although not an attestation of the entire story, a sword named {{nihongo|{{illm|Mukadegiri|ja|蜈蚣切}}|蚣切|extra2="Centepede-cutter"}} purportedly owned by Hidesato according to the inscription borne on its [[:en:Tang (tools)|tang]] was bequeathed to the [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Shrine]].{{r|yawata}} The Ise Shrine ({{illm|Jingū Chōkokan Museum|ja|神宮徴古館|lt=Chōkokan Museum}}) also houses a {{illm|kenuki gata|ja|毛抜形太刀|lt=''kenuki gata''}} or "tweezer type" that allegedly belonged to Hidesato.{{r|sato-kanzan}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The Chōkokan Museum editors surmised that this particular {{illm|Kenuki gata (Ise)|ja|毛抜形太刀 (重要文化財工第1354号)|lt=''kenuki gata'' sword (Ise)}} was the very sword that was heirloom to the {{illm|Akahori clan|ja|赤堀氏}}, to which was attached the legend of it being the gift of the Dragon Palace.{{r|jinguchokokan1941}}}}
[[File:Tatsu 辰(Dragon) (BM 2008,3037.06405).jpg|thumb|alt=Benkei draggin the bell|Benkei dragging the bell]]
There is a legendary incident concerning the bell donated by Tawara Tōda to Mii-dera', which was serving as the ''{{ill|Bonshō|en|Bonshō|WD=Q8192099|lt=Bonshō}}''-bell to tell the hour. It happened centuries later, when [[:en:Musashibō Benkei|Musashibō Benkei]] captured and dragged it up the mountain to  Eizan ([[Enryaku-ji]]), but the bell failed to toll properly. Thus the bell has been returned and has so remained at the rightful temple.<ref name=iwaya1914-eng/>{{sfnp|Junker von Langegg|1880|pp=155–156}}

=== Fairy tale translations ===
An English version of the tale entitled "My Lord Bag-O'-Rice" (1887) was translated by {{ill|Basil Hall Chamberlain|en|Basil Hall Chamberlain|WD=Q810029|lt=Basil Hall Chamberlain}}, and published as Japanese Fairy Tale Series No. 15 by {{ill|Hasegawa Takejirō|en|Hasegawa Takejirō|WD=Q5678771|lt=Hasegawa Takejirō}}.<ref>{{WorldCat|oclc=7082393|name=My lord Bag-o'-Rice'' (Basil Hall Chamberlain translation)}} (1887)</ref><ref>Reprint: {{citation|last=Chamberlain |first=Basil Hall |title=My lord Bag-o'-Rice |place=London and Sydney |publisher=ondon : Griffith, Farran & Co. ; Sidney |date=1892–1896 |url=https://archive.org/details/mylordbagorice00chamiala/}}</ref>

An ''otogibanashi'' (Japanese fairy tale) version entitled {{nihongo|”Tawara Tōda"||「俵藤太」 |extra2=}}, retold by {{illm|Iwaya Sazanami|ja|巌谷小波}} appeared in the 1890s.<ref>{{harvp|Iwaya|1896}}; {{harvp|Iwaya|1927|pp=147-158}}</ref> Subsequently, "My Lord Bag of Rice" was included in ''Japanese Fairy Tales'' (1903) anthologized by {{ill|Yei Theodora Ozaki|en|Yei Theodora Ozaki|WD=Q8051334|lt=Yei Theodora Ozaki}}.<ref>{{cite book|last=Ozaki|first=Yei Theodora |author-link=Yei Theodora Ozaki |chapter=My Lord Bag of Rice |title=Japanese Fairy Tales |location=Westminster |publisher=Archibald Constable & Co. |year=1903 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=V_RyPbadxJgC&pg=PA1|pages=1–11 }}</ref>{{r|dunne}} Ozaki's version is a retelling based on the rendition by "Sadanami sanjin",{{sfnp|Ozaki|1903|p=v}} the misspelled {{ill|pseudonym|en|pseudonym|WD=Q61002|lt=alias}} of Iwaya Sazanami.<ref>{{harvp|Herring|1988|p=100}}: "..»Sadanami«. This name is a misprint of the ''[[:en:nom de plume|nom de plume]]'' of Sazanami Iwaya".</ref> Ozaki's book was illustrated by Kakuzō Fujiyama.{{sfnp|Ozaki|1903|p=v}} Iwaya's version of several fairy tales were later collected, and {{ill|Hannah Riddell|en|Hannah Riddell|WD=Q5648947|lt=Hannah Riddell}}'s translation, "'''Tawara Toda Hidesato (''Hidesato of the Rice Bale'')'''".<ref name=iwaya1914-eng/>

"My Lord Bag of Rice" is also found in ''A Book of Dragons'' (1965) by {{ill|Ruth Manning-Sanders|en|Ruth Manning-Sanders|WD=Q4965445|lt=Ruth Manning-Sanders}}, illustrated by {{ill|Robin Jacques|en|Robin Jacques|WD=Q7352570|lt=Robin Jacques}}.<ref>{{cite book|last=Manning-Sanders |first=Ruth |author-link=Ruth Manning-Sanders |chapter=My Lord Bag of Rice |title=A Book of Dragons |publisher=Dutton |year=1965 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8HThAAAAMAAJ |pages=38–42|isbn=9780416581102 }}</ref>

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[en:Tawara Tōda Monogatari]][[id:Kisah Tawara Tōda]][[ru:Тавара Тода]][[sv:Tawara Toda]][[uk:Тавара Тода]]
<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[en:Tawara Tōda Monogatari]][[id:Kisah Tawara Tōda]][[ru:Тавара Тода]][[sv:Tawara Toda]][[uk:Тавара Тода]]
<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[en:Tawara Tōda Monogatari]][[id:Kisah Tawara Tōda]][[ru:Тавара Тода]][[sv:Tawara Toda]][[uk:Тавара Тода]]
{{Italic title}}
{{Short description|Japanese heroic fairy tale}}
[[Image:Kuniyoshi The Dragon Princess.jpg|thumb|240px|Dragon Woman and Tawara Tōda. Centipede of Mt. Mikami (above).{{right|{{small|―[[Utagawa Kuniyoshi]] 1845, ''Tokaidō gojūsantsui: Kusatsu''}}}}]]
[[Image:Yoshitoshi Fujiwara no Hidesato.jpg|thumb|200px|Hidesato aiming his shoot at the giant centipede.{{right|{{small|―{{ill|Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|en|Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|WD=Q467337|lt=Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|1=Tsukioka Yoshitoshi}} 1890.}}}}]]

{{nihongo|'''''The Tale of Tawara Tōda'''''|俵藤太物語|'''''Tawara Tōda monogatari'''''}} is a Japanese heroic tale recounting the legendary exploits of {{ill|Fujiwara no Hidesato|en|Fujiwara no Hidesato|WD=Q1136623|lt=Fujiwara no Hidesato|1=Fujiwara no Hidesato}}. It is part of the ''[[otogi-zōshi]]'' genre of tales dating to the [[:en:Edo Period|Edo Period]] or earlier. Some of the fabulous accounts are also told in the {{ill|Gunki monogatari|en|Gunki monogatari|WD=Q587327|lt=military pseudo-chronicle|1=Gunki monogatari}}, ''[[Taiheiki]]'' (14th century).

Hidesato used a {{ill|Bow and arrow|en|Bow and arrow|WD=Q19827042|lt=Bow and arrow|1=Bow and arrow}} to kill a giant centipede (''{{ill|ōmukade|en|ōmukade|WD=Q60788646|lt=mukade|1=Ōmukade}}'') wrapped around a mountain near {{ill|Lake Biwa|en|Lake Biwa|WD=Q200239|lt=Lake Biwa|1=Lake Biwa}}, fulfilling the request of a serpent at a bridge, which turned out to be a court lady (or Dragon King) from the underwater {{nihongo||龍宮城|[[Ryūgū-jō]]|extra2="Dragon Palace"}}. The hero was entertained at the palace and received rewards including armor and sword, and an inexhaustible bag of rice.{{efn|Or rice sack ({{illm|Tawara (container)|lt=''tawara''|ja|俵}}).}}

'''"My Lord Bag-O'-Rice"'''  is English-translated title of {{ill|Basil Hall Chamberlain|en|Basil Hall Chamberlain|WD=Q810029|lt=Basil Hall Chamberlain|1=Basil Hall Chamberlain}}'s retelling, published as a {{ill|Fairy tale|en|Fairy tale|WD=Q699|lt=Fairy tale|1=Fairy tale}} (1887). This was later followed by {{ill|Yei Theodora Ozaki|en|Yei Theodora Ozaki|WD=Q8051334|lt=Yei Theodora Ozaki|1=Yei Theodora Ozaki}}'s translation "'''My Lord Bag of Rice'''" (1903) based on {{illm|Iwaya Sazanami|ja|巌谷小波}}'s retelling.

== Setting ==
The story is set in {{ill|Ōmi Province|en|Ōmi Province|WD=Q843882|lt=Ōmi Province|1=Ōmi Province}} ({{ill|Shiga Prefecture|en|Shiga Prefecture|WD=Q131358|lt=Shiga Prefecture|1=Shiga Prefecture}}), and begins with a large serpent lying on {{illm|Seta Bridge|ja|瀬田の唐橋}} on the brink of {{ill|Lake Biwa|en|Lake Biwa|WD=Q200239|lt=Lake Biwa|1=Lake Biwa}}. The serpent, which later assumes human form, conveys Hidesato to the Dragon Palace, which can be reached through the depths of this Lake.{{sfnp|Kimbrough|2018}}{{sfnp|Visser|1913|pp=191–192}}

There is a Shinto shrine near the Seta Bridge at Lake Biwa where people have venerated Tawara Tōda.{{sfnp|Visser|1913|p=191}}

== Personage ==
{{nihongo|Tawara Tōda|俵藤太|extra=lit. 'Rice-bag Tōda'}} is a name that plays a {{ill|pun|en|pun|WD=Q263668|lt=pun|1=Pun}} between ''[[Wikt:tawara|tawara]]'' meaning 'straw rice-bag; straw barrel' and {{nihongo||Tawara|田原}}, a {{ill|proper noun|en|proper noun|WD=Q147276|lt=proper name|1=Proper noun}} (which may be a {{ill|Japanese name|en|Japanese name|WD=Q877834|lt=person's name|1=Japanese name}} or a place name). It was the nickname given to the historical {{ill|Fujiwara no Hidesato|en|Fujiwara no Hidesato|WD=Q1136623|lt=Fujiwara no Hidesato|1=Fujiwara no Hidesato}} who flourished in the first half of the 10th century and participated in the suppression of the rebel usurper {{ill|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado|2=en|3=Taira no Masakado|4=ja|5=平将門|6=de|7=Taira no Masakado|8=es|9=Taira no Masakado|10=fr|11=Taira no Masakado|lt=Taira no Masakado|WD=Q1207652|en|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado|2=en|3=Taira no Masakado|4=ja|5=平将門|6=de|7=Taira no Masakado|8=es|9=Taira no Masakado|10=fr|11=Taira no Masakado|lt=Taira no Masakado|WD=Q1207652|WD=Q1207652|lt=Taira no Masakado}}.<ref>{{harvp|Visser|1913|loc=p. 191, 192 and note 3}}</ref>

The nickname is sometimes styled "Tawara [no] Tōta".<ref name=foster/>

== Summary ==
The hero's centipede-slaying legend as contained in the ''Tawara Tōda monogatari'' ("The Tale of Tawara Tōda") was widely circulated and read during the early [[:en:Edo Period|Edo Period]] (17th century), when the text was being copied in picture scrolls (''[[:en:Emaki|Emaki]]'') and appearing in [[:en:Otogizōshi|Otogizōshi]] type woodblock-printed (and hand-copied) books.{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The Tawara Tōda story is not one of the 23 pieces listed in the more stringent definition of ''otogizōshi''. But it has been printed under the ''otogizōshi'' anthology.{{r|knbt19}} {{harvp|Araki|1981}} also discusses it as an ''otogizōshi'' narrative, in the broader sense.}}{{sfnp|Araki|1981|pp=1–2}}{{sfnp|Kimbrough|2018}} A summary of the ''monogatari'' version is as follows:

{{Block indent|1=
Fujiwara no Hidesato confronted the large serpent which lay on {{illm|Seta Bridge|ja|瀬田の唐橋}} in {{ill|Ōmi Province|en|Ōmi Province|WD=Q843882|lt=Ōmi Province|1=Ōmi Province}} disrupting travelers. Undaunted by this twelve horned snake measuring 200 feet,{{efn|20 ''jō'' ().}} the hero stepped on its back and crossed over, continuing onward. That night he was visited by a young woman who proclaimed to be the transformation of the serpent. Near {{ill|Lake Biwa|en|Lake Biwa|WD=Q200239|lt=Lake Biwa|1=Lake Biwa}} where she lived, a huge centipede took up residence on {{ill|Mount Mikami|en|Mount Mikami|WD=Q10865239|lt=Mount Mikami|1=Mount Mikami}}, and was devouring beasts and fish and even her own kindred.
}}
{{Block indent|1=Hidesato accepted her plea to eradicate this creature, and went to Seta. When the centipede came slinking down, it appeared as if two or three thousand torches were descending the mountain. Hidesato shot two arrows which failed to lodge, but when he laid spittle on the third arrow and prayed to his patron [[Hachiman]] deity it struck a grievous blow. Hidesato approached the creature{{Efn|Which had a head like an ox-demon (''[[gyūki]]'')}} and hacked it to pieces.{{Efn|Presumably with his heirloom sword which he had brought.}}
}}
{{Block indent|1=The dragon woman was elated and gave him magical gifts: undiminishing bolts of silk, inexhaustible rice bag, and a {{ill|Shakudō|en|Shakudō|WD=Q912435|lt=crimson copper|1=Shakudō}} pan of plenty (or "pot of alloyed gold and copper"{{sfnp|Dykstra|Kurata|2000|p=76}}). It was on account of the rice bag ({{illm|Tawara (container)|lt=''tawara''|ja|俵}}) that Hidesato received the nickname Tawara Tōda. The dragon woman took him to the Dragon-Palace ([[Ryūgū-jō|Ryūgū]]), where he was entertained and lavished with additional gifts from the Dragon King.{{Efn|The ''monogatari'' version elaborates that this was {{ill|Sāgara (Dragon King)|en|Sāgara (Dragon King)|WD=Q85804720|lt=Sāgara the Dragon King|1=Sāgara (Dragon King)}} who (in {{ill|Buddhism|en|Buddhism|WD=Q748|lt=Buddhism|1=Buddhism}}) was one of the {{illm|Eight Great Dragon Kings|ja|八大竜王}} (among the {{ill|Eight Legions|en|Eight Legions|WD=Q1045328|lt=Eight Legions|1=Eight Legions}}).}} Hidesato was given armor and sword, and a crimson copper bell. Hidesato subsequently donated this bell to {{ill|Mii-dera|en|Mii-dera|WD=Q1756307|lt=Mii-dera|1=Mii-dera}} temple at the foot of {{ill|Mount Hiei|en|Mount Hiei|WD=Q748040|lt=Mount Hiei|1=Mount Hiei}}.{{sfnp|Araki|1981|p=2}}{{sfnp|Kimbrough|2018}}{{r|knbt19}}{{efn|A legend concerning {{ill|Benkei|en|Benkei|WD=Q316898|lt=Benkei|1=Benkei}} is attached to the bell. See below.}}
}}

The ''monogatari'' version probably derives from earlier accounts of Hidesato's centipede slaying described in the 14th-century ''[[Taiheiki]]'', expanded with layers of legendary and religious (Buddhist) motifs.{{sfnp|Araki|1981|pp=3–4}} The above summary is not the entirety of ''Tawara Tōda monogatari'', which contains a second part where the hero triumphs over {{ill|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado|2=en|3=Taira no Masakado|4=ja|5=平将門|6=de|7=Taira no Masakado|8=es|9=Taira no Masakado|10=fr|11=Taira no Masakado|lt=Taira no Masakado|WD=Q1207652|en|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado|2=en|3=Taira no Masakado|4=ja|5=平将門|6=de|7=Taira no Masakado|8=es|9=Taira no Masakado|10=fr|11=Taira no Masakado|lt=Taira no Masakado|WD=Q1207652|WD=Q1207652|lt=Taira no Masakado}}, despite the latter having an iron body which was invulnerable except at the {{ill|Temple (anatomy)|en|Temple (anatomy)|WD=Q243999|lt=temples|1=Temple (anatomy)}} on his head, and having six ghostly doubles of himself.{{sfnp|Araki|1981|pp=3–4}}

=== Taiheiki version ===
The 14th-century ''[[Taiheiki]]'' records a much earlier version of this legend about Hidesato,<ref>''Taiheiki'', Book 15 [[:ja:s:太平記/巻第十五|太平記 巻第十五]], Chapter 118 "About the Battle of Miidera Temple, etc. 三井寺合戦並当寺撞鐘事付俵藤太事".</ref>{{sfnp|Dykstra|Kurata|2000|p=61}} but instead of the dragon turning into a beautiful woman, it transforms into a "strange small man"{{sfnp|Dykstra|Kurata|2000|p=61}} – the {{ill|Dragon King|en|Dragon King|WD=Q135337914|lt=Dragon King|1=Dragon King}} himself.{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|In the ''Taiheiki'' it is not explcit that the "small man" and the "Dragon God" (not "Dragon King" in original text) are the same personage, so this must be inferred. The small man changes into wearing a {{nihongo||冠|kanmuri|extra2="crown"}} but this headdress is worn by various officials, not just the monarch.}}{{sfnp|Visser|1913|p=192}}{{r|shigehara}} And here, Hidesato is invited to the Dragon Palace first and thereafter combats the centipede that attacks the aquatic realm.{{sfnp|Dykstra|Kurata|2000|p=61}}{{sfnp|Friday|2008|pp=157-158}} Here the inexhaustible silk and rice bag are received from the Dragon King,{{efn|Rather than the Dragon Woman, as in the ''monogatari'' version}} but not the copper alloy pan/pot, only the copper temple-bell.{{sfnp|Friday|2008|pp=157-158}}

=== Other attestations ===
{{Further|Fujiwara no Hidesato#Legendary arms}}

A version (similar to the ''monogatari'') appears in {{Nihongo||本朝怪談故事|Honchō kaidan koji}} (1711) as pointed out by Dutch Japanologist {{illm|Marinus Willem de Visser|de|Marinus Willem de Visser}}.{{sfnp|Visser|1913|pp=191–192}}

The centipede coiled seven and a half turns around Mount Mikami according to popular tradition.{{r|foster}} An early written mention of this occurs in the {{ill|chorography|en|chorography|WD=Q2088593|lt=area guidebook|1=Chorography}} ''Ōmi yochi shiryaku'' (1723).<ref>{{citation|last=Sangawa |first=Tokikiyo 寒川辰清 |script-title=ja:巻之卅九 秀郷社 |title=Book39: Hidesato (no) yashiro  |work=Ōmi yochi shiryaku 近江輿地志略 : 校定頭註 |publisher=Seinō Insatsu|year=1915|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/950934/284 |pages=466–468|language=ja}}</ref>

The name {{nihongo|Chikushi|遅来矢}} has been ascribed to the sword given by the Dragon King in the ''{{ill|Wakan Sansai Zue|en|Wakan Sansai Zue|WD=Q1135803|lt=Wakan sansai zue|1=Wakan Sansai Zue}}'' encyclopedia (1712) and the {{illm|Tōkaidō meisho zue|ja|東海道名所図会|lt=''Tōkaidō meisho zue''}} almanac (1797).{{Efn|This sword was passed down the {{illm|Akahori clan|ja|赤堀氏}}, these sources add.}}{{r|wakan-sansai-zue}}{{r|tokaido-meisho-zue}}<ref>Noted by {{harvp|Shida|1941|p=5}}</ref>

Hidesato's alleged armor from the Dragon Palace bore the similarly scripted name {{nihongo|Hiraishi|避来矢}} according to the ''Ujisatoki'' (before 1713{{r|owada}}).{{Efn|This armor was passed down {{illm|Sano clan|ja|佐野氏}} of {{ill|Shimotsuke Province|en|Shimotsuke Province|WD=Q1053699|lt=Shimotsuke Province|1=Shimotsuke Province}}, the ''Ujisatoki'' adds.}}<ref>{{harvp|Shida|1941|p=7}}: "the characters are extremely similar 文字が甚だよく似てゐる"</ref>{{r|ujisatoki-kondo}}<ref>Noted by {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|en|Minakata Kumagusu|WD=Q6862791|lt=Minakata Kumagusu|1=Minakata Kumagusu}} (1916) ''[https://www.aozora.gr.jp/cards/000093/files/1916_29070.html Jūnishikō: Tawara Tōda ryūgū-iri no hanashi 十二支考 田原藤太竜宮入りの話]''; {{harvp|Nakamura|1971|p=214}}</ref> {{nihongo|Hiraishi|平石}}, an armor with the {{ill|Homophone|en|Homophone|WD=Q221079|lt=same-sounding|1=Homophone}} but differently written name, is listed as a gift of Dragon Palace in [[Arai Hakuseki]]'s ''Honchō gunkikō'' (1709); this work mentions a second armor {{nihongo|Muromaru|室丸}} being obtained as well.{{r|honcho-gunkiko-armour}}<ref>Noted by {{harvp|Shida|1941|p=7}}; {{harvp|Nakamura|1971|p=214}}.</ref>

Although not an attestation of the entire story, a sword named {{nihongo|{{illm|Mukadegiri|ja|蜈蚣切}}|蚣切|extra2="Centepede-cutter"}} purportedly owned by Hidesato according to the inscription borne on its [[:en:Tang (tools)|tang]] was bequeathed to the [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Shrine]].{{r|yawata}} The Ise Shrine ({{illm|Jingū Chōkokan Museum|ja|神宮徴古館|lt=Chōkokan Museum}}) also houses a {{illm|kenuki gata|ja|毛抜形太刀|lt=''kenuki gata''}} or "tweezer type" that allegedly belonged to Hidesato.{{r|sato-kanzan}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The Chōkokan Museum editors surmised that this particular {{illm|Kenuki gata (Ise)|ja|毛抜形太刀 (重要文化財工第1354号)|lt=''kenuki gata'' sword (Ise)}} was the very sword that was heirloom to the {{illm|Akahori clan|ja|赤堀氏}}, to which was attached the legend of it being the gift of the Dragon Palace.{{r|jinguchokokan1941}}}}
[[File:Tatsu 辰(Dragon) (BM 2008,3037.06405).jpg|thumb|alt=Benkei draggin the bell|Benkei dragging the bell]]
There is a legendary incident concerning the bell donated by Tawara Tōda to Mii-dera', which was serving as the ''{{ill|Bonshō|en|Bonshō|WD=Q8192099|lt=Bonshō|1=Bonshō}}''-bell to tell the hour. It happened centuries later, when [[:en:Musashibō Benkei|Musashibō Benkei]] captured and dragged it up the mountain to  Eizan ([[Enryaku-ji]]), but the bell failed to toll properly. Thus the bell has been returned and has so remained at the rightful temple.<ref name=iwaya1914-eng/>{{sfnp|Junker von Langegg|1880|pp=155–156}}

=== Fairy tale translations ===
An English version of the tale entitled "My Lord Bag-O'-Rice" (1887) was translated by {{ill|Basil Hall Chamberlain|en|Basil Hall Chamberlain|WD=Q810029|lt=Basil Hall Chamberlain|1=Basil Hall Chamberlain}}, and published as Japanese Fairy Tale Series No. 15 by {{ill|Hasegawa Takejirō|en|Hasegawa Takejirō|WD=Q5678771|lt=Hasegawa Takejirō|1=Hasegawa Takejirō}}.<ref>{{WorldCat|oclc=7082393|name=My lord Bag-o'-Rice'' (Basil Hall Chamberlain translation)}} (1887)</ref><ref>Reprint: {{citation|last=Chamberlain |first=Basil Hall |title=My lord Bag-o'-Rice |place=London and Sydney |publisher=ondon : Griffith, Farran & Co. ; Sidney |date=1892–1896 |url=https://archive.org/details/mylordbagorice00chamiala/}}</ref>

An ''otogibanashi'' (Japanese fairy tale) version entitled {{nihongo|”Tawara Tōda"||「俵藤太」 |extra2=}}, retold by {{illm|Iwaya Sazanami|ja|巌谷小波}} appeared in the 1890s.<ref>{{harvp|Iwaya|1896}}; {{harvp|Iwaya|1927|pp=147-158}}</ref> Subsequently, "My Lord Bag of Rice" was included in ''Japanese Fairy Tales'' (1903) anthologized by {{ill|Yei Theodora Ozaki|en|Yei Theodora Ozaki|WD=Q8051334|lt=Yei Theodora Ozaki|1=Yei Theodora Ozaki}}.<ref>{{cite book|last=Ozaki|first=Yei Theodora |author-link=Yei Theodora Ozaki |chapter=My Lord Bag of Rice |title=Japanese Fairy Tales |location=Westminster |publisher=Archibald Constable & Co. |year=1903 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=V_RyPbadxJgC&pg=PA1|pages=1–11 }}</ref>{{r|dunne}} Ozaki's version is a retelling based on the rendition by "Sadanami sanjin",{{sfnp|Ozaki|1903|p=v}} the misspelled {{ill|pseudonym|en|pseudonym|WD=Q61002|lt=alias|1=Pseudonym}} of Iwaya Sazanami.<ref>{{harvp|Herring|1988|p=100}}: "..»Sadanami«. This name is a misprint of the ''[[:en:nom de plume|nom de plume]]'' of Sazanami Iwaya".</ref> Ozaki's book was illustrated by Kakuzō Fujiyama.{{sfnp|Ozaki|1903|p=v}} Iwaya's version of several fairy tales were later collected, and {{ill|Hannah Riddell|en|Hannah Riddell|WD=Q5648947|lt=Hannah Riddell|1=Hannah Riddell}}'s translation, "'''Tawara Toda Hidesato (''Hidesato of the Rice Bale'')'''".<ref name=iwaya1914-eng/>

"My Lord Bag of Rice" is also found in ''A Book of Dragons'' (1965) by {{ill|Ruth Manning-Sanders|en|Ruth Manning-Sanders|WD=Q4965445|lt=Ruth Manning-Sanders|1=Ruth Manning-Sanders}}, illustrated by {{ill|Robin Jacques|en|Robin Jacques|WD=Q7352570|lt=Robin Jacques|1=Robin Jacques}}.<ref>{{cite book|last=Manning-Sanders |first=Ruth |author-link=Ruth Manning-Sanders |chapter=My Lord Bag of Rice |title=A Book of Dragons |publisher=Dutton |year=1965 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8HThAAAAMAAJ |pages=38–42|isbn=9780416581102 }}</ref>

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[en:Tawara Tōda Monogatari]][[id:Kisah Tawara Tōda]][[ru:Тавара Тода]][[sv:Tawara Toda]][[uk:Тавара Тода]]
<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[en:Tawara Tōda Monogatari]][[id:Kisah Tawara Tōda]][[ru:Тавара Тода]][[sv:Tawara Toda]][[uk:Тавара Тода]]
<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[en:Tawara Tōda Monogatari]][[id:Kisah Tawara Tōda]][[ru:Тавара Тода]][[sv:Tawara Toda]][[uk:Тавара Тода]]
{{Italic title}}
{{Short description|Japanese heroic fairy tale}}
[[Image:Kuniyoshi The Dragon Princess.jpg|thumb|240px|Dragon Woman and Tawara Tōda. Centipede of Mt. Mikami (above).{{right|{{small|―[[Utagawa Kuniyoshi]] 1845, ''Tokaidō gojūsantsui: Kusatsu''}}}}]]
[[Image:Yoshitoshi Fujiwara no Hidesato.jpg|thumb|200px|Hidesato aiming his shoot at the giant centipede.{{right|{{small|―{{ill|Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|en|Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|WD=Q467337|lt=Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|1=Tsukioka Yoshitoshi}} 1890.}}}}]]

{{nihongo|'''''The Tale of Tawara Tōda'''''|俵藤太物語|'''''Tawara Tōda monogatari'''''}} is a Japanese heroic tale recounting the legendary exploits of {{ill|Fujiwara no Hidesato|en|Fujiwara no Hidesato|WD=Q1136623|lt=Fujiwara no Hidesato|1=Fujiwara no Hidesato}}. It is part of the ''[[otogi-zōshi]]'' genre of tales dating to the [[:en:Edo Period|Edo Period]] or earlier. Some of the fabulous accounts are also told in the {{ill|Gunki monogatari|en|Gunki monogatari|WD=Q587327|lt=military pseudo-chronicle|1=Gunki monogatari}}, ''[[Taiheiki]]'' (14th century).

Hidesato used a {{ill|Bow and arrow|en|Bow and arrow|WD=Q19827042|lt=Bow and arrow|1=Bow and arrow}} to kill a giant centipede (''{{ill|ōmukade|en|ōmukade|WD=Q60788646|lt=mukade|1=Ōmukade}}'') wrapped around a mountain near {{ill|Lake Biwa|en|Lake Biwa|WD=Q200239|lt=Lake Biwa|1=Lake Biwa}}, fulfilling the request of a serpent at a bridge, which turned out to be a court lady (or Dragon King) from the underwater {{nihongo||龍宮城|[[Ryūgū-jō]]|extra2="Dragon Palace"}}. The hero was entertained at the palace and received rewards including armor and sword, and an inexhaustible bag of rice.{{efn|Or rice sack ({{illm|Tawara (container)|lt=''tawara''|ja|俵}}).}}

'''"My Lord Bag-O'-Rice"'''  is English-translated title of {{ill|Basil Hall Chamberlain|en|Basil Hall Chamberlain|WD=Q810029|lt=Basil Hall Chamberlain|1=Basil Hall Chamberlain}}'s retelling, published as a {{ill|Fairy tale|en|Fairy tale|WD=Q699|lt=Fairy tale|1=Fairy tale}} (1887). This was later followed by {{ill|Yei Theodora Ozaki|en|Yei Theodora Ozaki|WD=Q8051334|lt=Yei Theodora Ozaki|1=Yei Theodora Ozaki}}'s translation "'''My Lord Bag of Rice'''" (1903) based on {{illm|Iwaya Sazanami|ja|巌谷小波}}'s retelling.

== Setting ==
The story is set in {{ill|Ōmi Province|en|Ōmi Province|WD=Q843882|lt=Ōmi Province|1=Ōmi Province}} ({{ill|Shiga Prefecture|en|Shiga Prefecture|WD=Q131358|lt=Shiga Prefecture|1=Shiga Prefecture}}), and begins with a large serpent lying on {{illm|Seta Bridge|ja|瀬田の唐橋}} on the brink of {{ill|Lake Biwa|en|Lake Biwa|WD=Q200239|lt=Lake Biwa|1=Lake Biwa}}. The serpent, which later assumes human form, conveys Hidesato to the Dragon Palace, which can be reached through the depths of this Lake.{{sfnp|Kimbrough|2018}}{{sfnp|Visser|1913|pp=191–192}}

There is a Shinto shrine near the Seta Bridge at Lake Biwa where people have venerated Tawara Tōda.{{sfnp|Visser|1913|p=191}}

== Personage ==
{{nihongo|Tawara Tōda|俵藤太|extra=lit. 'Rice-bag Tōda'}} is a name that plays a {{ill|pun|en|pun|WD=Q263668|lt=pun|1=Pun}} between ''[[Wikt:tawara|tawara]]'' meaning 'straw rice-bag; straw barrel' and {{nihongo||Tawara|田原}}, a {{ill|proper noun|en|proper noun|WD=Q147276|lt=proper name|1=Proper noun}} (which may be a {{ill|Japanese name|en|Japanese name|WD=Q877834|lt=person's name|1=Japanese name}} or a place name). It was the nickname given to the historical {{ill|Fujiwara no Hidesato|en|Fujiwara no Hidesato|WD=Q1136623|lt=Fujiwara no Hidesato|1=Fujiwara no Hidesato}} who flourished in the first half of the 10th century and participated in the suppression of the rebel usurper {{ill|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado|2=en|3=Taira no Masakado|4=ja|5=平将門|6=de|7=Taira no Masakado|8=es|9=Taira no Masakado|10=fr|11=Taira no Masakado|lt=Taira no Masakado|WD=Q1207652|en|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado|2=en|3=Taira no Masakado|4=ja|5=平将門|6=de|7=Taira no Masakado|8=es|9=Taira no Masakado|10=fr|11=Taira no Masakado|lt=Taira no Masakado|WD=Q1207652|WD=Q1207652|lt=Taira no Masakado}}.<ref>{{harvp|Visser|1913|loc=p. 191, 192 and note 3}}</ref>

The nickname is sometimes styled "Tawara [no] Tōta".<ref name=foster/>

== Summary ==
The hero's centipede-slaying legend as contained in the ''Tawara Tōda monogatari'' ("The Tale of Tawara Tōda") was widely circulated and read during the early [[:en:Edo Period|Edo Period]] (17th century), when the text was being copied in picture scrolls (''[[:en:Emaki|Emaki]]'') and appearing in [[:en:Otogizōshi|Otogizōshi]] type woodblock-printed (and hand-copied) books.{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The Tawara Tōda story is not one of the 23 pieces listed in the more stringent definition of ''otogizōshi''. But it has been printed under the ''otogizōshi'' anthology.{{r|knbt19}} {{harvp|Araki|1981}} also discusses it as an ''otogizōshi'' narrative, in the broader sense.}}{{sfnp|Araki|1981|pp=1–2}}{{sfnp|Kimbrough|2018}} A summary of the ''monogatari'' version is as follows:

{{Block indent|1=
Fujiwara no Hidesato confronted the large serpent which lay on {{illm|Seta Bridge|ja|瀬田の唐橋}} in {{ill|Ōmi Province|en|Ōmi Province|WD=Q843882|lt=Ōmi Province|1=Ōmi Province}} disrupting travelers. Undaunted by this twelve horned snake measuring 200 feet,{{efn|20 ''jō'' ().}} the hero stepped on its back and crossed over, continuing onward. That night he was visited by a young woman who proclaimed to be the transformation of the serpent. Near {{ill|Lake Biwa|en|Lake Biwa|WD=Q200239|lt=Lake Biwa|1=Lake Biwa}} where she lived, a huge centipede took up residence on {{ill|Mount Mikami|en|Mount Mikami|WD=Q10865239|lt=Mount Mikami|1=Mount Mikami}}, and was devouring beasts and fish and even her own kindred.
}}
{{Block indent|1=Hidesato accepted her plea to eradicate this creature, and went to Seta. When the centipede came slinking down, it appeared as if two or three thousand torches were descending the mountain. Hidesato shot two arrows which failed to lodge, but when he laid spittle on the third arrow and prayed to his patron [[Hachiman]] deity it struck a grievous blow. Hidesato approached the creature{{Efn|Which had a head like an ox-demon (''[[gyūki]]'')}} and hacked it to pieces.{{Efn|Presumably with his heirloom sword which he had brought.}}
}}
{{Block indent|1=The dragon woman was elated and gave him magical gifts: undiminishing bolts of silk, inexhaustible rice bag, and a {{ill|Shakudō|en|Shakudō|WD=Q912435|lt=crimson copper|1=Shakudō}} pan of plenty (or "pot of alloyed gold and copper"{{sfnp|Dykstra|Kurata|2000|p=76}}). It was on account of the rice bag ({{illm|Tawara (container)|lt=''tawara''|ja|俵}}) that Hidesato received the nickname Tawara Tōda. The dragon woman took him to the Dragon-Palace ([[Ryūgū-jō|Ryūgū]]), where he was entertained and lavished with additional gifts from the Dragon King.{{Efn|The ''monogatari'' version elaborates that this was {{ill|Sāgara (Dragon King)|en|Sāgara (Dragon King)|WD=Q85804720|lt=Sāgara the Dragon King|1=Sāgara (Dragon King)}} who (in {{ill|Buddhism|en|Buddhism|WD=Q748|lt=Buddhism|1=Buddhism}}) was one of the {{illm|Eight Great Dragon Kings|ja|八大竜王}} (among the {{ill|Eight Legions|en|Eight Legions|WD=Q1045328|lt=Eight Legions|1=Eight Legions}}).}} Hidesato was given armor and sword, and a crimson copper bell. Hidesato subsequently donated this bell to {{ill|Mii-dera|en|Mii-dera|WD=Q1756307|lt=Mii-dera|1=Mii-dera}} temple at the foot of {{ill|Mount Hiei|en|Mount Hiei|WD=Q748040|lt=Mount Hiei|1=Mount Hiei}}.{{sfnp|Araki|1981|p=2}}{{sfnp|Kimbrough|2018}}{{r|knbt19}}{{efn|A legend concerning {{ill|Benkei|en|Benkei|WD=Q316898|lt=Benkei|1=Benkei}} is attached to the bell. See below.}}
}}

The ''monogatari'' version probably derives from earlier accounts of Hidesato's centipede slaying described in the 14th-century ''[[Taiheiki]]'', expanded with layers of legendary and religious (Buddhist) motifs.{{sfnp|Araki|1981|pp=3–4}} The above summary is not the entirety of ''Tawara Tōda monogatari'', which contains a second part where the hero triumphs over {{ill|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado|2=en|3=Taira no Masakado|4=ja|5=平将門|6=de|7=Taira no Masakado|8=es|9=Taira no Masakado|10=fr|11=Taira no Masakado|lt=Taira no Masakado|WD=Q1207652|en|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado|2=en|3=Taira no Masakado|4=ja|5=平将門|6=de|7=Taira no Masakado|8=es|9=Taira no Masakado|10=fr|11=Taira no Masakado|lt=Taira no Masakado|WD=Q1207652|WD=Q1207652|lt=Taira no Masakado}}, despite the latter having an iron body which was invulnerable except at the {{ill|Temple (anatomy)|en|Temple (anatomy)|WD=Q243999|lt=temples|1=Temple (anatomy)}} on his head, and having six ghostly doubles of himself.{{sfnp|Araki|1981|pp=3–4}}

=== Taiheiki version ===
The 14th-century ''[[Taiheiki]]'' records a much earlier version of this legend about Hidesato,<ref>''Taiheiki'', Book 15 [[:ja:s:太平記/巻第十五|太平記 巻第十五]], Chapter 118 "About the Battle of Miidera Temple, etc. 三井寺合戦並当寺撞鐘事付俵藤太事".</ref>{{sfnp|Dykstra|Kurata|2000|p=61}} but instead of the dragon turning into a beautiful woman, it transforms into a "strange small man"{{sfnp|Dykstra|Kurata|2000|p=61}} – the {{ill|Dragon King|en|Dragon King|WD=Q135337914|lt=Dragon King|1=Dragon King}} himself.{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|In the ''Taiheiki'' it is not explcit that the "small man" and the "Dragon God" (not "Dragon King" in original text) are the same personage, so this must be inferred. The small man changes into wearing a {{nihongo||冠|kanmuri|extra2="crown"}} but this headdress is worn by various officials, not just the monarch.}}{{sfnp|Visser|1913|p=192}}{{r|shigehara}} And here, Hidesato is invited to the Dragon Palace first and thereafter combats the centipede that attacks the aquatic realm.{{sfnp|Dykstra|Kurata|2000|p=61}}{{sfnp|Friday|2008|pp=157-158}} Here the inexhaustible silk and rice bag are received from the Dragon King,{{efn|Rather than the Dragon Woman, as in the ''monogatari'' version}} but not the copper alloy pan/pot, only the copper temple-bell.{{sfnp|Friday|2008|pp=157-158}}

=== Other attestations ===
{{Further|Fujiwara no Hidesato#Legendary arms}}

A version (similar to the ''monogatari'') appears in {{Nihongo||本朝怪談故事|Honchō kaidan koji}} (1711) as pointed out by Dutch Japanologist {{illm|Marinus Willem de Visser|de|Marinus Willem de Visser}}.{{sfnp|Visser|1913|pp=191–192}}

The centipede coiled seven and a half turns around Mount Mikami according to popular tradition.{{r|foster}} An early written mention of this occurs in the {{ill|chorography|en|chorography|WD=Q2088593|lt=area guidebook|1=Chorography}} ''Ōmi yochi shiryaku'' (1723).<ref>{{citation|last=Sangawa |first=Tokikiyo 寒川辰清 |script-title=ja:巻之卅九 秀郷社 |title=Book39: Hidesato (no) yashiro  |work=Ōmi yochi shiryaku 近江輿地志略 : 校定頭註 |publisher=Seinō Insatsu|year=1915|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/950934/284 |pages=466–468|language=ja}}</ref>

The name {{nihongo|Chikushi|遅来矢}} has been ascribed to the sword given by the Dragon King in the ''{{ill|Wakan Sansai Zue|en|Wakan Sansai Zue|WD=Q1135803|lt=Wakan sansai zue|1=Wakan Sansai Zue}}'' encyclopedia (1712) and the {{illm|Tōkaidō meisho zue|ja|東海道名所図会|lt=''Tōkaidō meisho zue''}} almanac (1797).{{Efn|This sword was passed down the {{illm|Akahori clan|ja|赤堀氏}}, these sources add.}}{{r|wakan-sansai-zue}}{{r|tokaido-meisho-zue}}<ref>Noted by {{harvp|Shida|1941|p=5}}</ref>

Hidesato's alleged armor from the Dragon Palace bore the similarly scripted name {{nihongo|Hiraishi|避来矢}} according to the ''Ujisatoki'' (before 1713{{r|owada}}).{{Efn|This armor was passed down {{illm|Sano clan|ja|佐野氏}} of {{ill|Shimotsuke Province|en|Shimotsuke Province|WD=Q1053699|lt=Shimotsuke Province|1=Shimotsuke Province}}, the ''Ujisatoki'' adds.}}<ref>{{harvp|Shida|1941|p=7}}: "the characters are extremely similar 文字が甚だよく似てゐる"</ref>{{r|ujisatoki-kondo}}<ref>Noted by {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|en|Minakata Kumagusu|WD=Q6862791|lt=Minakata Kumagusu|1=Minakata Kumagusu}} (1916) ''[https://www.aozora.gr.jp/cards/000093/files/1916_29070.html Jūnishikō: Tawara Tōda ryūgū-iri no hanashi 十二支考 田原藤太竜宮入りの話]''; {{harvp|Nakamura|1971|p=214}}</ref> {{nihongo|Hiraishi|平石}}, an armor with the {{ill|Homophone|en|Homophone|WD=Q221079|lt=same-sounding|1=Homophone}} but differently written name, is listed as a gift of Dragon Palace in [[Arai Hakuseki]]'s ''Honchō gunkikō'' (1709); this work mentions a second armor {{nihongo|Muromaru|室丸}} being obtained as well.{{r|honcho-gunkiko-armour}}<ref>Noted by {{harvp|Shida|1941|p=7}}; {{harvp|Nakamura|1971|p=214}}.</ref>

Although not an attestation of the entire story, a sword named {{nihongo|{{illm|Mukadegiri|ja|蜈蚣切}}|蚣切|extra2="Centepede-cutter"}} purportedly owned by Hidesato according to the inscription borne on its [[:en:Tang (tools)|tang]] was bequeathed to the [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Shrine]].{{r|yawata}} The Ise Shrine ({{illm|Jingū Chōkokan Museum|ja|神宮徴古館|lt=Chōkokan Museum}}) also houses a {{illm|kenuki gata|ja|毛抜形太刀|lt=''kenuki gata''}} or "tweezer type" that allegedly belonged to Hidesato.{{r|sato-kanzan}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The Chōkokan Museum editors surmised that this particular {{illm|Kenuki gata (Ise)|ja|毛抜形太刀 (重要文化財工第1354号)|lt=''kenuki gata'' sword (Ise)}} was the very sword that was heirloom to the {{illm|Akahori clan|ja|赤堀氏}}, to which was attached the legend of it being the gift of the Dragon Palace.{{r|jinguchokokan1941}}}}
[[File:Tatsu 辰(Dragon) (BM 2008,3037.06405).jpg|thumb|alt=Benkei draggin the bell|Benkei dragging the bell]]
There is a legendary incident concerning the bell donated by Tawara Tōda to Mii-dera', which was serving as the ''{{ill|Bonshō|en|Bonshō|WD=Q8192099|lt=Bonshō|1=Bonshō}}''-bell to tell the hour. It happened centuries later, when [[:en:Musashibō Benkei|Musashibō Benkei]] captured and dragged it up the mountain to  Eizan ([[Enryaku-ji]]), but the bell failed to toll properly. Thus the bell has been returned and has so remained at the rightful temple.<ref name=iwaya1914-eng/>{{sfnp|Junker von Langegg|1880|pp=155–156}}

=== Fairy tale translations ===
An English version of the tale entitled "My Lord Bag-O'-Rice" (1887) was translated by {{ill|Basil Hall Chamberlain|en|Basil Hall Chamberlain|WD=Q810029|lt=Basil Hall Chamberlain|1=Basil Hall Chamberlain}}, and published as Japanese Fairy Tale Series No. 15 by {{ill|Hasegawa Takejirō|en|Hasegawa Takejirō|WD=Q5678771|lt=Hasegawa Takejirō|1=Hasegawa Takejirō}}.<ref>{{WorldCat|oclc=7082393|name=My lord Bag-o'-Rice'' (Basil Hall Chamberlain translation)}} (1887)</ref><ref>Reprint: {{citation|last=Chamberlain |first=Basil Hall |title=My lord Bag-o'-Rice |place=London and Sydney |publisher=ondon : Griffith, Farran & Co. ; Sidney |date=1892–1896 |url=https://archive.org/details/mylordbagorice00chamiala/}}</ref>

An ''otogibanashi'' (Japanese fairy tale) version entitled {{nihongo|”Tawara Tōda"||「俵藤太」 |extra2=}}, retold by {{illm|Iwaya Sazanami|ja|巌谷小波}} appeared in the 1890s.<ref>{{harvp|Iwaya|1896}}; {{harvp|Iwaya|1927|pp=147-158}}</ref> Subsequently, "My Lord Bag of Rice" was included in ''Japanese Fairy Tales'' (1903) anthologized by {{ill|Yei Theodora Ozaki|en|Yei Theodora Ozaki|WD=Q8051334|lt=Yei Theodora Ozaki|1=Yei Theodora Ozaki}}.<ref>{{cite book|last=Ozaki|first=Yei Theodora |author-link=Yei Theodora Ozaki |chapter=My Lord Bag of Rice |title=Japanese Fairy Tales |location=Westminster |publisher=Archibald Constable & Co. |year=1903 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=V_RyPbadxJgC&pg=PA1|pages=1–11 }}</ref>{{r|dunne}} Ozaki's version is a retelling based on the rendition by "Sadanami sanjin",{{sfnp|Ozaki|1903|p=v}} the misspelled {{ill|pseudonym|en|pseudonym|WD=Q61002|lt=alias|1=Pseudonym}} of Iwaya Sazanami.<ref>{{harvp|Herring|1988|p=100}}: "..»Sadanami«. This name is a misprint of the ''[[:en:nom de plume|nom de plume]]'' of Sazanami Iwaya".</ref> Ozaki's book was illustrated by Kakuzō Fujiyama.{{sfnp|Ozaki|1903|p=v}} Iwaya's version of several fairy tales were later collected, and {{ill|Hannah Riddell|en|Hannah Riddell|WD=Q5648947|lt=Hannah Riddell|1=Hannah Riddell}}'s translation, "'''Tawara Toda Hidesato (''Hidesato of the Rice Bale'')'''".<ref name=iwaya1914-eng/>

"My Lord Bag of Rice" is also found in ''A Book of Dragons'' (1965) by {{ill|Ruth Manning-Sanders|en|Ruth Manning-Sanders|WD=Q4965445|lt=Ruth Manning-Sanders|1=Ruth Manning-Sanders}}, illustrated by {{ill|Robin Jacques|en|Robin Jacques|WD=Q7352570|lt=Robin Jacques|1=Robin Jacques}}.<ref>{{cite book|last=Manning-Sanders |first=Ruth |author-link=Ruth Manning-Sanders |chapter=My Lord Bag of Rice |title=A Book of Dragons |publisher=Dutton |year=1965 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8HThAAAAMAAJ |pages=38–42|isbn=9780416581102 }}</ref>

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[en:Tawara Tōda Monogatari]][[id:Kisah Tawara Tōda]][[ru:Тавара Тода]][[sv:Tawara Toda]][[uk:Тавара Тода]]
{{Italic title}}
{{Short description|Japanese heroic fairy tale}}
[[Image:Kuniyoshi The Dragon Princess.jpg|thumb|240px|Dragon Woman and Tawara Tōda. Centipede of Mt. Mikami (above).{{right|{{small|―[[Utagawa Kuniyoshi]] 1845, ''Tokaidō gojūsantsui: Kusatsu''}}}}]]
[[Image:Yoshitoshi Fujiwara no Hidesato.jpg|thumb|200px|Hidesato aiming his shoot at the giant centipede.{{right|{{small|―{{ill|Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|en|Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|WD=Q467337|lt=Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|1=Tsukioka Yoshitoshi}} 1890.}}}}]]

{{nihongo|'''''The Tale of Tawara Tōda'''''|俵藤太物語|'''''Tawara Tōda monogatari'''''}} is a Japanese heroic tale recounting the legendary exploits of {{ill|Fujiwara no Hidesato|en|Fujiwara no Hidesato|WD=Q1136623|lt=Fujiwara no Hidesato|1=Fujiwara no Hidesato}}. It is part of the ''[[otogi-zōshi]]'' genre of tales dating to the [[:en:Edo Period|Edo Period]] or earlier. Some of the fabulous accounts are also told in the {{ill|Gunki monogatari|en|Gunki monogatari|WD=Q587327|lt=military pseudo-chronicle|1=Gunki monogatari}}, ''[[Taiheiki]]'' (14th century).

Hidesato used a {{ill|Bow and arrow|en|Bow and arrow|WD=Q19827042|lt=Bow and arrow|1=Bow and arrow}} to kill a giant centipede (''{{ill|ōmukade|en|ōmukade|WD=Q60788646|lt=mukade|1=Ōmukade}}'') wrapped around a mountain near {{ill|Lake Biwa|en|Lake Biwa|WD=Q200239|lt=Lake Biwa|1=Lake Biwa}}, fulfilling the request of a serpent at a bridge, which turned out to be a court lady (or Dragon King) from the underwater {{nihongo||龍宮城|[[Ryūgū-jō]]|extra2="Dragon Palace"}}. The hero was entertained at the palace and received rewards including armor and sword, and an inexhaustible bag of rice.{{efn|Or rice sack ({{illm|Tawara (container)|lt=''tawara''|ja|俵}}).}}

'''"My Lord Bag-O'-Rice"'''  is English-translated title of {{ill|Basil Hall Chamberlain|en|Basil Hall Chamberlain|WD=Q810029|lt=Basil Hall Chamberlain|1=Basil Hall Chamberlain}}'s retelling, published as a {{ill|Fairy tale|en|Fairy tale|WD=Q699|lt=Fairy tale|1=Fairy tale}} (1887). This was later followed by {{ill|Yei Theodora Ozaki|en|Yei Theodora Ozaki|WD=Q8051334|lt=Yei Theodora Ozaki|1=Yei Theodora Ozaki}}'s translation "'''My Lord Bag of Rice'''" (1903) based on {{illm|Iwaya Sazanami|ja|巌谷小波}}'s retelling.

== Setting ==
The story is set in {{ill|Ōmi Province|en|Ōmi Province|WD=Q843882|lt=Ōmi Province|1=Ōmi Province}} ({{ill|Shiga Prefecture|en|Shiga Prefecture|WD=Q131358|lt=Shiga Prefecture|1=Shiga Prefecture}}), and begins with a large serpent lying on {{illm|Seta Bridge|ja|瀬田の唐橋}} on the brink of {{ill|Lake Biwa|en|Lake Biwa|WD=Q200239|lt=Lake Biwa|1=Lake Biwa}}. The serpent, which later assumes human form, conveys Hidesato to the Dragon Palace, which can be reached through the depths of this Lake.{{sfnp|Kimbrough|2018}}{{sfnp|Visser|1913|pp=191–192}}

There is a Shinto shrine near the Seta Bridge at Lake Biwa where people have venerated Tawara Tōda.{{sfnp|Visser|1913|p=191}}

== Personage ==
{{nihongo|Tawara Tōda|俵藤太|extra=lit. 'Rice-bag Tōda'}} is a name that plays a {{ill|pun|en|pun|WD=Q263668|lt=pun|1=Pun}} between ''[[Wikt:tawara|tawara]]'' meaning 'straw rice-bag; straw barrel' and {{nihongo||Tawara|田原}}, a {{ill|proper noun|en|proper noun|WD=Q147276|lt=proper name|1=Proper noun}} (which may be a {{ill|Japanese name|en|Japanese name|WD=Q877834|lt=person's name|1=Japanese name}} or a place name). It was the nickname given to the historical {{ill|Fujiwara no Hidesato|en|Fujiwara no Hidesato|WD=Q1136623|lt=Fujiwara no Hidesato|1=Fujiwara no Hidesato}} who flourished in the first half of the 10th century and participated in the suppression of the rebel usurper {{ill|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado|2=en|3=Taira no Masakado|4=ja|5=平将門|6=de|7=Taira no Masakado|8=es|9=Taira no Masakado|10=fr|11=Taira no Masakado|lt=Taira no Masakado|WD=Q1207652|en|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado|2=en|3=Taira no Masakado|4=ja|5=平将門|6=de|7=Taira no Masakado|8=es|9=Taira no Masakado|10=fr|11=Taira no Masakado|lt=Taira no Masakado|WD=Q1207652|WD=Q1207652|lt=Taira no Masakado}}.<ref>{{harvp|Visser|1913|loc=p. 191, 192 and note 3}}</ref>

The nickname is sometimes styled "Tawara [no] Tōta".<ref name=foster/>

== Summary ==
The hero's centipede-slaying legend as contained in the ''Tawara Tōda monogatari'' ("The Tale of Tawara Tōda") was widely circulated and read during the early [[:en:Edo Period|Edo Period]] (17th century), when the text was being copied in picture scrolls (''[[:en:Emaki|Emaki]]'') and appearing in [[:en:Otogizōshi|Otogizōshi]] type woodblock-printed (and hand-copied) books.{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The Tawara Tōda story is not one of the 23 pieces listed in the more stringent definition of ''otogizōshi''. But it has been printed under the ''otogizōshi'' anthology.{{r|knbt19}} {{harvp|Araki|1981}} also discusses it as an ''otogizōshi'' narrative, in the broader sense.}}{{sfnp|Araki|1981|pp=1–2}}{{sfnp|Kimbrough|2018}} A summary of the ''monogatari'' version is as follows:

{{Block indent|1=
Fujiwara no Hidesato confronted the large serpent which lay on {{illm|Seta Bridge|ja|瀬田の唐橋}} in {{ill|Ōmi Province|en|Ōmi Province|WD=Q843882|lt=Ōmi Province|1=Ōmi Province}} disrupting travelers. Undaunted by this twelve horned snake measuring 200 feet,{{efn|20 ''jō'' ().}} the hero stepped on its back and crossed over, continuing onward. That night he was visited by a young woman who proclaimed to be the transformation of the serpent. Near {{ill|Lake Biwa|en|Lake Biwa|WD=Q200239|lt=Lake Biwa|1=Lake Biwa}} where she lived, a huge centipede took up residence on {{ill|Mount Mikami|en|Mount Mikami|WD=Q10865239|lt=Mount Mikami|1=Mount Mikami}}, and was devouring beasts and fish and even her own kindred.
}}
{{Block indent|1=Hidesato accepted her plea to eradicate this creature, and went to Seta. When the centipede came slinking down, it appeared as if two or three thousand torches were descending the mountain. Hidesato shot two arrows which failed to lodge, but when he laid spittle on the third arrow and prayed to his patron [[Hachiman]] deity it struck a grievous blow. Hidesato approached the creature{{Efn|Which had a head like an ox-demon (''[[gyūki]]'')}} and hacked it to pieces.{{Efn|Presumably with his heirloom sword which he had brought.}}
}}
{{Block indent|1=The dragon woman was elated and gave him magical gifts: undiminishing bolts of silk, inexhaustible rice bag, and a {{ill|Shakudō|en|Shakudō|WD=Q912435|lt=crimson copper|1=Shakudō}} pan of plenty (or "pot of alloyed gold and copper"{{sfnp|Dykstra|Kurata|2000|p=76}}). It was on account of the rice bag ({{illm|Tawara (container)|lt=''tawara''|ja|俵}}) that Hidesato received the nickname Tawara Tōda. The dragon woman took him to the Dragon-Palace ([[Ryūgū-jō|Ryūgū]]), where he was entertained and lavished with additional gifts from the Dragon King.{{Efn|The ''monogatari'' version elaborates that this was {{ill|Sāgara (Dragon King)|en|Sāgara (Dragon King)|WD=Q85804720|lt=Sāgara the Dragon King|1=Sāgara (Dragon King)}} who (in {{ill|Buddhism|en|Buddhism|WD=Q748|lt=Buddhism|1=Buddhism}}) was one of the {{illm|Eight Great Dragon Kings|ja|八大竜王}} (among the {{ill|Eight Legions|en|Eight Legions|WD=Q1045328|lt=Eight Legions|1=Eight Legions}}).}} Hidesato was given armor and sword, and a crimson copper bell. Hidesato subsequently donated this bell to {{ill|Mii-dera|en|Mii-dera|WD=Q1756307|lt=Mii-dera|1=Mii-dera}} temple at the foot of {{ill|Mount Hiei|en|Mount Hiei|WD=Q748040|lt=Mount Hiei|1=Mount Hiei}}.{{sfnp|Araki|1981|p=2}}{{sfnp|Kimbrough|2018}}{{r|knbt19}}{{efn|A legend concerning {{ill|Benkei|en|Benkei|WD=Q316898|lt=Benkei|1=Benkei}} is attached to the bell. See below.}}
}}

The ''monogatari'' version probably derives from earlier accounts of Hidesato's centipede slaying described in the 14th-century ''[[Taiheiki]]'', expanded with layers of legendary and religious (Buddhist) motifs.{{sfnp|Araki|1981|pp=3–4}} The above summary is not the entirety of ''Tawara Tōda monogatari'', which contains a second part where the hero triumphs over {{ill|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado|2=en|3=Taira no Masakado|4=ja|5=平将門|6=de|7=Taira no Masakado|8=es|9=Taira no Masakado|10=fr|11=Taira no Masakado|lt=Taira no Masakado|WD=Q1207652|en|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado|2=en|3=Taira no Masakado|4=ja|5=平将門|6=de|7=Taira no Masakado|8=es|9=Taira no Masakado|10=fr|11=Taira no Masakado|lt=Taira no Masakado|WD=Q1207652|WD=Q1207652|lt=Taira no Masakado}}, despite the latter having an iron body which was invulnerable except at the {{ill|Temple (anatomy)|en|Temple (anatomy)|WD=Q243999|lt=temples|1=Temple (anatomy)}} on his head, and having six ghostly doubles of himself.{{sfnp|Araki|1981|pp=3–4}}

=== Taiheiki version ===
The 14th-century ''[[Taiheiki]]'' records a much earlier version of this legend about Hidesato,<ref>''Taiheiki'', Book 15 [[:ja:s:太平記/巻第十五|太平記 巻第十五]], Chapter 118 "About the Battle of Miidera Temple, etc. 三井寺合戦並当寺撞鐘事付俵藤太事".</ref>{{sfnp|Dykstra|Kurata|2000|p=61}} but instead of the dragon turning into a beautiful woman, it transforms into a "strange small man"{{sfnp|Dykstra|Kurata|2000|p=61}} – the {{ill|Dragon King|en|Dragon King|WD=Q135337914|lt=Dragon King|1=Dragon King}} himself.{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|In the ''Taiheiki'' it is not explcit that the "small man" and the "Dragon God" (not "Dragon King" in original text) are the same personage, so this must be inferred. The small man changes into wearing a {{nihongo||冠|kanmuri|extra2="crown"}} but this headdress is worn by various officials, not just the monarch.}}{{sfnp|Visser|1913|p=192}}{{r|shigehara}} And here, Hidesato is invited to the Dragon Palace first and thereafter combats the centipede that attacks the aquatic realm.{{sfnp|Dykstra|Kurata|2000|p=61}}{{sfnp|Friday|2008|pp=157-158}} Here the inexhaustible silk and rice bag are received from the Dragon King,{{efn|Rather than the Dragon Woman, as in the ''monogatari'' version}} but not the copper alloy pan/pot, only the copper temple-bell.{{sfnp|Friday|2008|pp=157-158}}

=== Other attestations ===
{{Further|Fujiwara no Hidesato#Legendary arms}}

A version (similar to the ''monogatari'') appears in {{Nihongo||本朝怪談故事|Honchō kaidan koji}} (1711) as pointed out by Dutch Japanologist {{illm|Marinus Willem de Visser|de|Marinus Willem de Visser}}.{{sfnp|Visser|1913|pp=191–192}}

The centipede coiled seven and a half turns around Mount Mikami according to popular tradition.{{r|foster}} An early written mention of this occurs in the {{ill|chorography|en|chorography|WD=Q2088593|lt=area guidebook|1=Chorography}} ''Ōmi yochi shiryaku'' (1723).<ref>{{citation|last=Sangawa |first=Tokikiyo 寒川辰清 |script-title=ja:巻之卅九 秀郷社 |title=Book39: Hidesato (no) yashiro  |work=Ōmi yochi shiryaku 近江輿地志略 : 校定頭註 |publisher=Seinō Insatsu|year=1915|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/950934/284 |pages=466–468|language=ja}}</ref>

The name {{nihongo|Chikushi|遅来矢}} has been ascribed to the sword given by the Dragon King in the ''{{ill|Wakan Sansai Zue|en|Wakan Sansai Zue|WD=Q1135803|lt=Wakan sansai zue|1=Wakan Sansai Zue}}'' encyclopedia (1712) and the {{illm|Tōkaidō meisho zue|ja|東海道名所図会|lt=''Tōkaidō meisho zue''}} almanac (1797).{{Efn|This sword was passed down the {{illm|Akahori clan|ja|赤堀氏}}, these sources add.}}{{r|wakan-sansai-zue}}{{r|tokaido-meisho-zue}}<ref>Noted by {{harvp|Shida|1941|p=5}}</ref>

Hidesato's alleged armor from the Dragon Palace bore the similarly scripted name {{nihongo|Hiraishi|避来矢}} according to the ''Ujisatoki'' (before 1713{{r|owada}}).{{Efn|This armor was passed down {{illm|Sano clan|ja|佐野氏}} of {{ill|Shimotsuke Province|en|Shimotsuke Province|WD=Q1053699|lt=Shimotsuke Province|1=Shimotsuke Province}}, the ''Ujisatoki'' adds.}}<ref>{{harvp|Shida|1941|p=7}}: "the characters are extremely similar 文字が甚だよく似てゐる"</ref>{{r|ujisatoki-kondo}}<ref>Noted by {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|en|Minakata Kumagusu|WD=Q6862791|lt=Minakata Kumagusu|1=Minakata Kumagusu}} (1916) ''[https://www.aozora.gr.jp/cards/000093/files/1916_29070.html Jūnishikō: Tawara Tōda ryūgū-iri no hanashi 十二支考 田原藤太竜宮入りの話]''; {{harvp|Nakamura|1971|p=214}}</ref> {{nihongo|Hiraishi|平石}}, an armor with the {{ill|Homophone|en|Homophone|WD=Q221079|lt=same-sounding|1=Homophone}} but differently written name, is listed as a gift of Dragon Palace in [[Arai Hakuseki]]'s ''Honchō gunkikō'' (1709); this work mentions a second armor {{nihongo|Muromaru|室丸}} being obtained as well.{{r|honcho-gunkiko-armour}}<ref>Noted by {{harvp|Shida|1941|p=7}}; {{harvp|Nakamura|1971|p=214}}.</ref>

Although not an attestation of the entire story, a sword named {{nihongo|{{illm|Mukadegiri|ja|蜈蚣切}}|蚣切|extra2="Centepede-cutter"}} purportedly owned by Hidesato according to the inscription borne on its [[:en:Tang (tools)|tang]] was bequeathed to the [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Shrine]].{{r|yawata}} The Ise Shrine ({{illm|Jingū Chōkokan Museum|ja|神宮徴古館|lt=Chōkokan Museum}}) also houses a {{illm|kenuki gata|ja|毛抜形太刀|lt=''kenuki gata''}} or "tweezer type" that allegedly belonged to Hidesato.{{r|sato-kanzan}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The Chōkokan Museum editors surmised that this particular {{illm|Kenuki gata (Ise)|ja|毛抜形太刀 (重要文化財工第1354号)|lt=''kenuki gata'' sword (Ise)}} was the very sword that was heirloom to the {{illm|Akahori clan|ja|赤堀氏}}, to which was attached the legend of it being the gift of the Dragon Palace.{{r|jinguchokokan1941}}}}
[[File:Tatsu 辰(Dragon) (BM 2008,3037.06405).jpg|thumb|alt=Benkei draggin the bell|Benkei dragging the bell]]
There is a legendary incident concerning the bell donated by Tawara Tōda to Mii-dera', which was serving as the ''{{ill|Bonshō|en|Bonshō|WD=Q8192099|lt=Bonshō|1=Bonshō}}''-bell to tell the hour. It happened centuries later, when [[:en:Musashibō Benkei|Musashibō Benkei]] captured and dragged it up the mountain to  Eizan ([[Enryaku-ji]]), but the bell failed to toll properly. Thus the bell has been returned and has so remained at the rightful temple.<ref name=iwaya1914-eng/>{{sfnp|Junker von Langegg|1880|pp=155–156}}

=== Fairy tale translations ===
An English version of the tale entitled "My Lord Bag-O'-Rice" (1887) was translated by {{ill|Basil Hall Chamberlain|en|Basil Hall Chamberlain|WD=Q810029|lt=Basil Hall Chamberlain|1=Basil Hall Chamberlain}}, and published as Japanese Fairy Tale Series No. 15 by {{ill|Hasegawa Takejirō|en|Hasegawa Takejirō|WD=Q5678771|lt=Hasegawa Takejirō|1=Hasegawa Takejirō}}.<ref>{{WorldCat|oclc=7082393|name=My lord Bag-o'-Rice'' (Basil Hall Chamberlain translation)}} (1887)</ref><ref>Reprint: {{citation|last=Chamberlain |first=Basil Hall |title=My lord Bag-o'-Rice |place=London and Sydney |publisher=ondon : Griffith, Farran & Co. ; Sidney |date=1892–1896 |url=https://archive.org/details/mylordbagorice00chamiala/}}</ref>

An ''otogibanashi'' (Japanese fairy tale) version entitled {{nihongo|”Tawara Tōda"||「俵藤太」 |extra2=}}, retold by {{illm|Iwaya Sazanami|ja|巌谷小波}} appeared in the 1890s.<ref>{{harvp|Iwaya|1896}}; {{harvp|Iwaya|1927|pp=147-158}}</ref> Subsequently, "My Lord Bag of Rice" was included in ''Japanese Fairy Tales'' (1903) anthologized by {{ill|Yei Theodora Ozaki|en|Yei Theodora Ozaki|WD=Q8051334|lt=Yei Theodora Ozaki|1=Yei Theodora Ozaki}}.<ref>{{cite book|last=Ozaki|first=Yei Theodora |author-link=Yei Theodora Ozaki |chapter=My Lord Bag of Rice |title=Japanese Fairy Tales |location=Westminster |publisher=Archibald Constable & Co. |year=1903 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=V_RyPbadxJgC&pg=PA1|pages=1–11 }}</ref>{{r|dunne}} Ozaki's version is a retelling based on the rendition by "Sadanami sanjin",{{sfnp|Ozaki|1903|p=v}} the misspelled {{ill|pseudonym|en|pseudonym|WD=Q61002|lt=alias|1=Pseudonym}} of Iwaya Sazanami.<ref>{{harvp|Herring|1988|p=100}}: "..»Sadanami«. This name is a misprint of the ''[[:en:nom de plume|nom de plume]]'' of Sazanami Iwaya".</ref> Ozaki's book was illustrated by Kakuzō Fujiyama.{{sfnp|Ozaki|1903|p=v}} Iwaya's version of several fairy tales were later collected, and {{ill|Hannah Riddell|en|Hannah Riddell|WD=Q5648947|lt=Hannah Riddell|1=Hannah Riddell}}'s translation, "'''Tawara Toda Hidesato (''Hidesato of the Rice Bale'')'''".<ref name=iwaya1914-eng/>

"My Lord Bag of Rice" is also found in ''A Book of Dragons'' (1965) by {{ill|Ruth Manning-Sanders|en|Ruth Manning-Sanders|WD=Q4965445|lt=Ruth Manning-Sanders|1=Ruth Manning-Sanders}}, illustrated by {{ill|Robin Jacques|en|Robin Jacques|WD=Q7352570|lt=Robin Jacques|1=Robin Jacques}}.<ref>{{cite book|last=Manning-Sanders |first=Ruth |author-link=Ruth Manning-Sanders |chapter=My Lord Bag of Rice |title=A Book of Dragons |publisher=Dutton |year=1965 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8HThAAAAMAAJ |pages=38–42|isbn=9780416581102 }}</ref>
